item.title: Court sentences Tahir Hussain to 2 years in jail for abetment in Delhi riots case
item.content:encoded:
A Delhi court on Friday sentenced former Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) councillor Tahir Hussain to two years' imprisonment after convicting him of abetment to rioting in a case related to 2020 Delhi riots.

Additional Sessions Judge Praveen Singh of the Karkardooma Court also imposed a cost of ₹10,000 on Hussain, who is already serving life imprisonment in the Ankit Sharma murder case.

"The act attributed to the convict, and for which he stands convicted, is that of providing his house to the rioters for their use. The mere fact that the prosecution did not prove the active participation of the convict in the riot, does not dilute the gravity of his conduct, for the hand that guides is as guilty, if not more, as the hand that acts," the Court said.

The Court had convicted Hussain on October 10, while acquitting all other accused in the case.

The FIR in the case was registered under Sections 147, 148, 149, 427, 436, 120B of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) at Dayalpur police station.

One Irshad Ali had filed the complaint alleging that his shop was looted and set on fire on February 24, 2020, causing losses of ₹17–18 lakh in stolen goods and ₹10 lakh in property damage. Another complainant, Mohd Zahid, said rioters raised slogans in support of Tahir Hussain, whom two constables identified during the investigation.

Special Public Prosecutor (SPP) Madhukar Pandey appeared for the State.

Tahir Hussain was represented through advocate Rajiv Mohan.

item.title: Detained on arrival: Section 172 BNSS and the borrowed power to stop a protest
item.media:keywords: Police,Detention,Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023,Delhi Protests,Section 172 BNSS
item.content:encoded:
On October 10, 2026, a protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar was supposed to take place. For many who set out to participate in this protest, the trip was cut short on the railway platform itself. People travelling to Delhi for the protest were reportedly detained in several States before they even reached the capital.

In Madhya Pradesh, at least 30 people were taken off trains and were detained at Bhopal, Gwalior and Itarsi. In Delhi itself, the police had imposed prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which bars assemblies of five or more, processions and dharnas without prior written permission.

None of this is new. What is new is the provision the State now uses to justify it. When the Uttarakhand High Court asked, in July, under what law an activist on his way to an earlier protest at Jantar Mantar had been taken off a train at Rishikesh, the State’s answer was Section 172 of the BNSS. That answer deserves scrutiny, because Section 172 does not carry the power it is being asked to carry. It is a power to enforce a police officer’s own directions within one narrow chapter of the Sanhita. It is being used to enforce a magistrate’s order made under another chapter, against the people who have not even reached the place that the order covers.

A new power with a narrow door

Section 172(1) binds all persons to “conform to the lawful directions of a police officer given in fulfilment of any of his duty under this Chapter.” Section 172(2) allows the officer to “detain or remove” anyone “resisting, refusing, ignoring or disregarding” such a direction, and then either take that person before a magistrate or, “in petty cases”, release them within 24 hours. The previous statute, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, had no equivalent provision. Detention for disobeying a police direction is a new addition in the BNSS.

The operative phrase is “under this Chapter”. Section 172 is present in Chapter XII, “Preventive Action of the Police”, which runs from Section 168 to Section 172. The duties it contains are: to prevent cognizable offences (Section 168), to pass on information of a design to commit one (Section 169), to arrest where that design is known and the offence cannot otherwise be prevented (Section 170) and to prevent injury to public property (Section 171). A direction under Section 172 must be given in fulfilment of one of these duties. It is not a free-standing power to order the public.

Borrowing from the wrong chapter

Section 163 orders are situated elsewhere. They are present in Chapter XI, titled Maintenance of Public Order and Tranquillity, and they are a magistrate’s orders, not a police officer’s directions. Parliament gave Chapter XI its own tools: dispersal of an assembly under Section 148 and prosecution for disobeying a duly promulgated order under Section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023. What it does not provide is the power to detain a person in advance or a person who is hundreds of kilometres away who might breach the Section 163 order later on. To find that power in Section 172, one must read “this Chapter” as “this Sanhita”.

The State’s defence in Lal Mani v. State of Uttarakhand shows how the borrowing is being done. The counsel for the State argued that disobeying a Section 163 order is a cognizable offence that can be committed anywhere in the country, so the police actions were only to prevent an offence. On that reasoning, the prospect of breaching a Chapter XI order triggers the Chapter XII duty under Section 168 and Section 172 does the rest. The Uttarakhand High Court asked the question which unravels it: what lawful direction had the man disobeyed? The bench further added that any offence in Delhi fell within the jurisdiction of the Delhi Police, not the Uttarakhand Police. Its order of July 20 had already framed the first question as one of which provision of law authorised the detention at all.

The circularity is the main point. If the only offence being prevented is disobedience of the order, the only direction that is being enforced is “do not go”. Section 172 does not empower a police officer to issue that direction, detain anyone who breaches it and then point to the breach as the duty that justified the direction. The direction must originate from a duty that exists independently of it.

The safeguard Section 172 bypasses

Chapter XII already contains a power to arrest in order to prevent a cognizable offence. Section 170 allows it only where the officer knows of “a design to commit” the offence and it seems that the offence “cannot be otherwise prevented”. Section 170 carries the old Section 151 of the CrPC without substantive change. In Rajender Singh Pathania v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2011), the Supreme Court held that an arrest under Section 151 of the CrPC is supportable only when its conditions are actually met. A student boarding a train to attend a protest at a designated site does not, on any ordinary reading, form a design to commit a cognizable offence. Neither is there anything to prove that his presence, if he defied the order on arrival, could not be dealt with there under Chapter XI.

Release as a way to dodge review

The second feature of Section 172(2) makes the first worse. Article 22(2) of the Constitution requires that every person who is arrested and detained in custody be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours. Section 172(2) allows the officer to release the person without producing them before a magistrate in “petty cases” within the same 24 hours. “Petty cases” is not defined. In reality, the detention ends before any magistrate sees it and the detainee leaves without a record that a court can test.

Lal Mani shows the same. By the time the High Court took up the habeas corpus petition, the activist had been released and the State said that he had been handed over to his mother’s custody. However, the bench refused to close the matter. It called for the full record of the detention and, the next day, sought the response of the officer who had detained the activist. Most people who were taken off trains before October 10 had no one to file a petition for them within hours. For them, release within 24 hours is not a safeguard. It only ensures that no court ever asks the question.

What the text needs

Three consequences follow. First, a Section 172 detention needs an identifiable direction, given to that person and traceable to a duty under Sections 168 to 171. If no direction is on record, the detention cannot stand. That is the question the Uttarakhand High Court bench asked first.

Second, when the objective is to stop someone from committing an offence, the State must satisfy Section 170 and must not take a route around it.

Third, a Section 163 order must be enforced at the place and time it covers, through the remedies Chapter XI provides, not by intercepting travellers in another State.

Reports from several States point to the same pattern. Even if only some of them are true, they point to mass use of a provision that is just over two years old and almost none of it will reach a court. Section 172 gives the police the power to move a crowd along. It should not be read to empower them to tell a citizen to stay at home.

Aarush Giri is a second-year BBA LLB (Hons.) student at Chandigarh University UP, Lucknow.

item.title: The void marriage and the invisible widow: Why the law needs an equitable answer
item.media:keywords: Hindu Succession Act,void marriage,Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
item.content:encoded:
A woman can spend her adult life with a man, raise his children, run his household and give up her career, and still walk away with nothing the day he dies, because a court later finds the marriage void.

This recurs whenever a marriage falls foul of Section 5, read with Section 11, of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA). The woman never becomes a wife in the eyes of law, so she can never become a widow either. And the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (HSA) has no room for her.

The answer is not to pretend the marriage was valid. It lies in something the HMA already accepts: that the legal fate of a relationship and its economic consequences need not be tied together. Section 16 legitimises children of void and voidable marriages without validating the marriage. The same idea can be extended, carefully and narrowly, to the woman who lived the marriage in good faith.

The statutory bind

Section 5(i) requires that neither party have a living spouse at the time of marriage. Section 11 declares a marriage in breach void from inception (Section 12 covers voidable marriages), so the woman never becomes a wife.

Section 8 of the HSA sends a Hindu male's intestate property first to his Class I heirs, which include the widow. But “widow” assumes a marriage that existed and ended in death. The Supreme Court said so in Rameshwari Devi v. State of Bihar (2000) where the second wife of a man whose earlier marriage was subsisting was denied any share as a widow. As statutory construction, this is unimpeachable. The problem is what follows: the woman is left with no legal identity in relation to the man she lived with for years, sometimes decades.

What Section 16 already teaches us

In Revanasiddappa v. Mallikarjun (2023), a three-judge bench held that children of void and voidable marriages, legitimised by Section 16, are entitled to their parents' property, including the share the parent would get on a notional partition of coparcenary property. While such children do not become coparceners by birth, they cannot be denied that share once it crystallises.

This departs from the stricter position in Jinia Keotin v. Kumar Sitaram Manjhi (2003), which confined such children to self-acquired property. This shift shows how the Court moved from treating Section 16 as a narrow savings clause to a genuine protective provision. The Court did not need to call the marriage valid to protect its children. It separated marital validity from who bears the economic consequences of the relationship. If that works for children, it can work for the mother who raised them.

The woman was never left entirely unprotected

Outside succession, courts have moved far towards protecting women in void or informal marriages during the man's lifetime. In Chanmuniya v. Virendra Kumar Singh Kushwaha (2011), the Supreme Court read “wife” broadly for maintenance: a woman who had lived with a man for a reasonable time in a marriage-like relationship could not be turned away for a technical defect. Badshah v. Urmila Badshah Godse (2014) sharpened this: the husband had concealed his first marriage,and the Court refused to let him use the defect he created to escape maintenance, so that a wrongdoer would not profit from his own wrong.

The Domestic Violence Act, 2005 built relationships “in the nature of marriage” into Section 2(f), with tests laid down in D Velusamy v. D Patchaiammal (2010) and Indra Sarma v. VKV Sarma (2013). Most recently, in Sukhdev Singh v. Sukhbir Kaur (2025), a three-judge bench held that a Section 11 decree still qualifies for Section 25 of the HMA, so a spouse in a void marriage can claim permanent alimony. The Court rejected the argument that a void marriage is non-existent for every purpose, leaving relief to the family court's discretion.

After the man's death, High Courts have at times allowed a second wife in a technically void marriage to draw a family pension where cohabitation was long, the first wife made no competing claim and refusal would leave her destitute. The family pension disputes involving second wives show how often this arises and how inconsistently it is resolved, with some benches demanding strict proof of marriage and others looking past the defect where dependence is undisputed.

The contradiction the law has not faced up to

While the man is alive, a woman in a void marriage may get maintenance, interim relief, Domestic Violence Act protection and even permanent alimony. The moment he dies, all of this protection disappears and the same relationship that was economically significant a day earlier becomes legally irrelevant.

Maintenance and succession serve different purposes - ongoing need versus distribution of an estate - but that does not explain why dependence stops mattering exactly when she needs help most. The case for protection is strongest then, as her household comes apart. The asymmetry is harder still to defend against the children. A child of the same void marriage inherits under Section 16 and Revanasiddappa. The mother, equally kept in the dark, inherits nothing.

Testing the exclusion against Article 14 and Article 21

The distinction between a valid and a void marriage is not itself irrational. The State may legitimately discourage bigamy and protect the lawfully wedded wife, and nothing here dilutes that. What is hard to defend is the consequence: a blanket exclusion that does not distinguish between a woman who knowingly entered a bigamous marriage and one who was deceived into it, and treats decades of cohabitation, dependence and household contribution as irrelevant.

Equality jurisprudence, from EP Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) to Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), holds that arbitrariness is itself a form of inequality. A rule can survive classification and still fail because its consequences are disproportionate to its objective. Denying every such woman any protection, regardless of good faith, duration or dependence, does little additional work in protecting monogamy once maintenance and alimony are available during his lifetime. Article 21's guarantee of dignity reinforces the point. A woman who discovers, at her point of greatest vulnerability, that thirty years of shared life count for nothing is not being denied a status. She is being denied the material means to live with dignity.

A way forward without rewriting Section 11

Courts should not stretch “widow” to cover women in void marriages, nor treat void marriages as valid. Both would weaken the prohibition on bigamy and endanger the lawfully wedded wife and legitimate children.

A narrower path exists in the reasoning courts have used for maintenance, alimony and family pension. A statutory entitlement, separate from Class I heirship, could be created for a woman who can show that a marriage ceremony took place and was later found void under Section 11; that she had no knowledge of the impediment; that the parties cohabited for a substantial, defined period; that the deceased held her out as his spouse; and that she is now genuinely dependent. Her claim would rank below the lawfully wedded widow and legitimate children, so the existing hierarchy of succession remains intact.

It extends the logic that family pension jurisprudence around second wives has been working out in the High Courts and that the Supreme Court applied to maintenance in Chanmuniya and Badshah, to alimony in Sukhdev Singh and to inheritance for children in Revanasiddappa. Succession is the last major area of Hindu family law still holding out against this trend and it is not obvious why it should.

Conclusion

Rameshwari Devi remains correctly decided on the law as it stands and this piece does not argue for overturning it. The point is narrower. The complete legal invisibility of a woman in a void marriage, after decades of shared life, is not compelled by the objective of preserving monogamy, which is already protected by denying her the status of wife and widow. What she should not lose, in addition, is every means of economic support because the relationship that sustained her turned out to be void.

A bounded, equity-based entitlement, kept below the rights of the lawfully wedded widow and her children, would let the law hold two ideas together: that a void marriage never becomes a valid one and that a woman who lived it in good faith should not be left with nothing the day it ends.

Vedant Dhakad is an LL.M. scholar and Anubha Shukla is a third-year student at Gujarat National Law University, Gandhinagar.

item.title: We will sit on dharna till you fix pedestrian crossing issue on Mathura road: Supreme Court in lighter vein
item.media:keywords: Delhi High Court,Supreme Court of India,NCT of Delhi,Justice JB Pardiwala,Dharna,Pedestrian Safety,Justice KV Viswanathan
item.content:encoded:
A bench of Supreme Court Justices JB Pardiwala and KV Viswanathan on Friday quipped that they would sit on a protest (dharna) at the main gate of the Delhi High Court if concrete measures are not taken to ensure pedestrian safety on Mathura Road before November 25.

The bench expressed dissatisfaction over delays in fixing the dangerous pedestrian crossing near the Delhi High Court junction and the National Zoological Park, where thousands of lawyers, litigants, and children cross daily.

While addressing Additional Solicitor General (ASG) Vikramjit Banerjee, said, the Court, in a lighter vein, said,

"If you don't do it before the next date, both of us will be at the main gate of the Delhi High Court, and we will not go home until you complete the work. That's for sure. Baith jaayenge wahan dharna karne ke liye baith jaayenge (We will sit there on dharna), and we will not allow Mr. Banerjee (ASG) to also go home."

Banerjee responded that a committee was actively looking into the issue after discussions at the highest levels. However, the Court questioned the bureaucratic delay in fixing a basic traffic bottleneck.

"Why do you need a committee for this? You need some engineers? You take Mr. Gaurav Agarwal [amicus curiae], he will help you. Why do you need a high-level committee? Include Mr. Agarwal in the committee. He will show what’s the exact problem over there," it observed.

Issuing a strict deadline, the Court made it clear that bureaucratic explanations would no longer suffice.

"But it has to be completed before 25th November. That’s for sure. No solution. Concrete work to be completed. Otherwise your Chief Secretary will be here beside you. Understood?" the Bench warned.

Supreme CourtIf you don't do it before the next date, both of us will be at the main gate of the Delhi High Court, and we will not go home until you complete the work.

In October 2025 and September 2026, the Court had flagged the absence of functional red lights, foot overbridges, or traffic-calming measures on the high-density Mathura road stretch.

Although a pedestrian signal was installed following court orders, amicus curiae Gaurav Agrawal informed the bench that it frequently remains non-functional, necessitating synchronized signals and speed-limiting rumble strips.

The matter will now be heard on November 25.

The Court's remarks – even though on the lighter side, come at a time when the national capital has been witnessing a flurry of street protests.
